title: Ritual Purity, Food, Table Fellowship, and Idol Food
summary: A passage-controlled evidence cluster that distinguishes Levitical impurity and food categories, Jewish legal diversity, gentile inclusion, shared-table pressures, cultic participation, market food, conscience, and the different arguments of Mark 7, Acts 10-15, Romans 14, and 1 Corinthians 8-10.
historical_context: Jewish food, purity, and table practices in the late Second Temple period were rooted in Torah but interpreted diversely. Early Christ-following assemblies brought Jews and gentiles into unequal Roman households, markets, associations, and cultic environments where eating could express kinship, status, hospitality, economic dependence, or ritual participation.
ancient_near_east_context: Leviticus supplies the principal ancient Israelite categories. Generic ancient Near Eastern comparison does not control the first-century disputes, which require Second Temple Jewish, Roman civic, household, market, and cultic evidence.
hebraic_worldview: Clean and unclean, holy and common, sacrifice, idolatry, covenant identity, Israel and the nations, and care for another person's conscience are relational categories embedded in Israel's Scriptures. They are not interchangeable labels for dirtiness, personal guilt, ethnicity, or human worth.
second_temple_context: 4QMMT, purity-oriented material culture, and later rabbinic collections show sustained Jewish legal reasoning and differentiated practice. Each source is geographically, socially, and chronologically bounded; none authorizes a portrait of Judaism as one legalistic system.
canonical_context: Mark 7 narrates an internal Jewish dispute about hand impurity, inherited practice, divine command, and defilement. Acts 10-11 interprets Peter's animal vision through gentile persons, hospitality, proclamation, and Spirit reception; Acts 15 addresses gentile circumcision and communal obligations. Romans 14-15 and 1 Corinthians 8-10 address different assemblies and different food conflicts. Shared vocabulary does not make them one universal dietary code.
later_christian_reception: These passages have been used both to welcome across ethnic boundaries and to demean Jewish observance, pressure people to violate conscience, or impose new food taboos. Responsible reception rejects antisemitism, forced eating, purity-based stigma, and the assumption that hospitality requires unsafe or coerced consumption.
literary_context: The cluster moves from Torah instruction to Gospel controversy, repeated vision-and-speech narrative, council speech and letter, and two Pauline deliberative arguments. Narrative symbols, textual variants, rhetorical slogans, case distinctions, and exhortations must remain distinguishable.
covenantal_significance: The passages negotiate holiness, Israel's Scriptures, gentile belonging, idolatry, and shared communal life without making Jewish covenant practice a moral defect. Competing theological syntheses remain interpretations rather than historical data.
date_ranges: Levitical traditions and final literary formation: debated across the first millennium BCE
Mishnah Yadayim: approximately 190-230 CE and later comparative

Codex Bezae: approximately fifth century CE witness to an earlier textual tradition
original_audience: Readers comparing food, purity, gentile inclusion, conscience, and idolatry passages without erasing their distinct settings or Jewish contexts.
historical_setting: Ancient Israelite priestly instruction; late Second Temple Jewish legal practice; and early Roman Jewish-gentile assemblies in Galilee, Judea, Caesarea, Antioch, Rome, and Corinth.
canonical_role: This cluster joins direct passage observations to dated legal, material, textual, and meal comparisons while keeping description, reconstruction, and theological application separate.

interpretive_notes.note: Ritual impurity can be temporary and nonculpable; do not turn clean/unclean terminology into a ranking of human dignity.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Levitical causes, remedies, and sanctions differ, while scholarly taxonomies remain models.

interpretive_notes.note: Mark 7 is an internal Jewish legal controversy. Neither the opponents nor Jewish food practice should be caricatured as hypocrisy, dirt anxiety, or salvation by rule keeping.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The scene appeals to Torah and inherited practice within a Jewish narrative world.

interpretive_notes.note: Acts 10 explicitly applies common and unclean language to people in Peter's speech; a dietary implication may be debated but must not displace the narrated gentile-inclusion outcome.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The narrative interprets the vision through Peter's visit, proclamation, Spirit reception, and retelling.

interpretive_notes.note: Conscience language does not authorize leaders, hosts, employers, or majorities to shame or force another person to eat, abstain, disclose trauma, or enter a cultic or unsafe setting.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Both Pauline arguments restrict self-assertion when another participant is endangered.

interpretive_notes.note: Do not merge Mark 7, Acts 10-15, Romans 14, and 1 Corinthians 8-10 into one timeless menu. Each passage names different actors, problems, rhetorical moves, and social settings.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Canonical comparison is legitimate only after distinct literary evidence is preserved.

claims.claim: Leviticus differentiates temporary bodily impurity and purification from prohibited conduct that defiles people, sanctuary, or land, even though the categories interact.
claims.rationale: Causes, durations, rites, sanctions, and vocabulary differ; modern labels remain analytic models.
claims.notes: Unclean does not automatically mean sinful or inferior.

claims.claim: Leviticus 11 distinguishes animals permitted for Israel to eat from carcass-contact impurity and joins these instructions to holiness without reducing every food prohibition to transmissible ritual impurity.
claims.rationale: Textual distinctions are explicit; rationale and taxonomy differ.
claims.notes: No modern hygiene theory is encoded as the law's single purpose.

claims.claim: 4QMMT, stone-vessel production, and later Mishnah Yadayim attest serious purity practice and legal reasoning without demonstrating one uniform Jewish standard across periods.
claims.rationale: Texts and artifacts are secure but differ in date, place, group, and representativeness.
claims.notes: None identifies Mark's disputants or the Jerusalem assembly.

claims.claim: Mark 7 begins with some disciples eating bread with common or unwashed hands and then moves through inherited practice, divine command, ingestion, and moral defilement.
claims.rationale: The trigger and sequence are explicit; Mark's generalizations and redaction remain disputed.
claims.notes: No prohibited animal is named in the meal.

claims.claim: The masculine participle in Mark 7:19 is well attested, but narrator-comment, digestive-argument, and limited-food readings remain disputed.
claims.rationale: Manuscript, syntax, punctuation, discourse, and Jewish legal context support competing readings.
claims.notes: No translation is treated as interpretation-free.

claims.claim: Mark 7 locates listed harmful actions in the human heart and contrasts them with ingested material, while ritual and moral impurity remain related but analytically distinct.
claims.rationale: The contrast and vice list are explicit; legal scope is interpreted.
claims.notes: The moral focus does not license stigma toward bodies or food traditions.

claims.claim: Acts 10 narrates a repeated command to kill and eat, Peter's refusal based on common and unclean food, a divine cleansing response, and Peter's continuing perplexity.
claims.rationale: The sequence is explicit; event history and symbolic scope remain interpreted.
claims.notes: Peter does not immediately state a dietary conclusion.

claims.claim: Peter says God showed him not to call any person common or unclean, enters Cornelius's gentile home, proclaims, and witnesses Spirit reception.
claims.rationale: The human application and outcome are explicit; historical reconstruction remains separate.
claims.notes: Gentile welcome does not make Jewish identity or practice impure.

claims.claim: Acts 11 retells the vision and visit, climaxes with Spirit reception, and reports recognition that God granted gentiles repentance leading to life.
claims.rationale: The retelling and response are direct observations; speech history is narrated.
claims.notes: The gentile-inclusion outcome remains central.

claims.claim: Acts 15 frames the Jerusalem dispute around whether gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses, then narrates debate, testimony, Scripture, and a written decision.
claims.rationale: The framing is explicit; historical relation to Paul's letters remains disputed.
claims.notes: Torah observance by Jews is not the problem under deliberation.

claims.claim: The dominant Acts text gives four gentile abstentions, while Western witnesses transmit a shorter ethicalized form; Leviticus 17-18, idolatry, shared tables, and gentile ethics remain competing background explanations.
claims.rationale: The readings are observable; genealogy, lexical scope, and rationale remain disputed.
claims.notes: No reconstructed source becomes a universal modern menu.

claims.claim: Galatians 2 reports withdrawal from gentile table fellowship at Antioch, while Acts 15 narrates a Jerusalem decision about gentiles; their sequence, motives, and agreement cannot be fully recovered.
claims.rationale: Both texts attest conflict around gentiles and meals; harmonization requires uncertain chronology.
claims.notes: Do not assign collective blame beyond what each text states.

claims.claim: Romans 14 names eating, abstention, vegetables, days, wine, judgment, and welcome but does not fully identify the weak and strong by ethnicity, class, or prior cult.
claims.rationale: Practices and labels are explicit; demographic equations are reconstructed.
claims.notes: Weak is not permission to demean observant or vulnerable people.

claims.claim: Paul says nothing is common in itself while accommodating contrary conviction and frames the dispute through mutual welcome, divine judgment, and service to the Lord.
claims.rationale: The language is explicit; relation to kashrut and Jesus tradition is debated.
claims.notes: Paul's lexical choice koinos remains visible.

claims.claim: Romans 14 subordinates food and wine claims to love, peace, upbuilding, avoidance of stumbling, and protection of the person for whom Messiah died.
claims.rationale: The constraints are direct; modern extension requires safety judgment.
claims.notes: Self-denial cannot be weaponized by the powerful.

claims.claim: First Corinthians 8 contrasts knowledge that puffs up with love that builds up and describes former idol association, conscience, visible temple dining, and harm.
claims.rationale: The contrasts are explicit; slogans, faction identities, and status are debated.
claims.notes: Former cult participation may involve dependence, grief, or trauma.

claims.claim: First Corinthians affirms one God and one Lord while prohibiting cultic table participation, distinguishing an idol's status from the social-ritual act of sacrifice and dining.
claims.rationale: Both moves occur in the argument; metaphysics, rhetoric, and venues are debated.
claims.notes: The evidence does not authorize harm toward other worshipers.

claims.claim: First Corinthians 10 differentiates market food, an unbeliever's private invitation, and a meal where someone identifies sacrificial provenance, with different instructions tied to conscience.
claims.rationale: Settings and conditional disclosure are explicit; supply chain and informant identity remain disputed.
claims.notes: Not every Corinthian meal or piece of meat is presumed sacrificial.

claims.claim: P.Oxy. 1.110 preserves a second-century Egyptian invitation to dine in connection with Sarapis, showing that cult-associated dining invitations could take ordinary social form.
claims.rationale: The papyrus is secure; it is later, Egyptian, and not the exact Corinthian meal.
claims.notes: Cult and private dining can overlap without becoming identical.

claims.claim: Mark 7, Acts 10-15, Romans 14, and 1 Corinthians 8-10 use food and purity language for distinct disputes and do not present one identical audience, menu, rationale, or rule form.
claims.rationale: Distinct literary sequences are observable even where canonical theology relates them.
claims.notes: Synthesis follows rather than erases passage-level interpretation.

evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Scholars distinguish ritual and moral impurity while debating overlap and development.

evidence_items.confidence_rationale: Readings are observable, but genealogy, priority, lexical scope, and legal derivation are disputed.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: Preserves the actual variants before deriving Leviticus 17-18, table fellowship, idolatry, Noahide comparison, or universal ethics.
evidence_items.primary_observation: Acts repeats a fourfold dominant form; D 05 witnesses a shorter ethicalized form.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Text critics debate development, while legal historians dispute which scriptural and Jewish obligations explain the list.

evidence_items.title: Gentile tables in Galatians 2 and Acts 15
evidence_items.description: Paul reports an Antiochene withdrawal from gentile tables; Acts narrates Jerusalem deliberation and a decree concerning gentiles.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: Both witnesses are strong, but chronology, sequence, motives, participants, and relationship are disputed.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: Shows why food rules affect embodied belonging while blocking a seamless harmonized council narrative.
evidence_items.primary_observation: Galatians says Paul opposed Cephas after withdrawal; Acts narrates debate and a letter to gentiles.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Reconstructions place the incident around different Jerusalem visits and explain withdrawal in varied ways.

evidence_items.title: Romans 14 names practices but underdetermines identities
evidence_items.description: Romans names omnivorous eating, vegetables, days, abstention, wine, judgment, and welcome without a complete profile of each side.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: Practices are explicit; identities, motives, trigger, and setting are disputed.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: Blocks automatic equations of weak with Jews, strong with gentiles, or vegetable eating with idol-meat fear alone.
evidence_items.primary_observation: Romans 14 names eating everything, vegetables, days, wine, common food, conscience, and stumbling.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Proposals emphasize Jewish practice, asceticism, Roman status, market uncertainty, or mixed causes.

scripture_references.relevance_rationale: The passage names practices while leaving identities incomplete.

evidence_items.title: Common food, conviction, and mutual welcome

evidence_items.confidence_rationale: Wording is explicit; source and dietary scope remain debated.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: Prevents verse 14 becoming a coercive slogan detached from welcome and judgment warnings.
evidence_items.primary_observation: Romans 14:3 prohibits despising and judging; verse 14 uses koinos while recognizing conviction.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Scholars debate kashrut, Jesus tradition, conscience, and Paul's practice.

evidence_items.description: First Corinthians 8 places idol claims beside love, prior idol association, conscience, visible temple dining, and harm.

evidence_items.title: One God, idol claims, and prohibited cultic participation
evidence_items.description: First Corinthians distinguishes claims about idols and the one God and Lord from cultic participation incompatible with the Lord's table.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: Both moves are explicit; slogans, demon language, ritual ontology, and venues are disputed.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: Explains why Paul can deny an idol's independent status yet reject a cultic meal without making every market purchase the same act.
evidence_items.primary_observation: First Corinthians 8:4-6 speaks of idol nonexistence and one God and Lord; 10:16-22 uses participation, sacrifice, cup, and table.

evidence_items.title: Market purchase, private invitation, and disclosed provenance

evidence_items.title: P.Oxy. 1.110 and a later Sarapis invitation
evidence_items.description: A second-century Egyptian papyrus invites its recipient to dine at the table of Sarapis in an ordinary social form.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: Papyrus, genre, and association are secure; date precision, venue, and Corinthian comparability are limited.

evidence_items.primary_observation: P.Oxy. I 110 is a personal invitation naming dining at the table of Sarapis and a time.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Scholars compare such invitations with temple and household dining while noting varied venues.

evidence_items.title: Distinct passage arguments resist a universal menu
evidence_items.description: Mark, Acts, Romans, and First Corinthians organize food and purity around different disputes, actors, settings, and outcomes.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: Literary differences are explicit; canonical syntheses remain diverse and contested.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: Requires passage-level interpretation before any verse becomes a timeless diet rule or cancels another text.

evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Scholars relate them through Torah, gentile mission, Jesus tradition, Pauline ethics, and development while disputing continuity.

hermeneutical_lens.immediate_literary_context: Read each food or purity statement inside its local dispute, case sequence, and narrated outcome.
hermeneutical_lens.book_context: Leviticus, Mark, Acts, Romans, and First Corinthians use different genres and address different communities.
hermeneutical_lens.canonical_context: Relate passages only after preserving vocabulary, chronology, and rhetorical differences.
hermeneutical_lens.covenant_context: Jewish covenant practice and gentile inclusion must not be framed as worth versus legalism.
hermeneutical_lens.historical_context: Use Jewish, Roman household, market, cultic, manuscript, and papyrological evidence within date and place limits.
hermeneutical_lens.ancient_near_east_context: Do not substitute generic ANE comparison for direct Israelite and first-century evidence.
hermeneutical_lens.second_temple_jewish_context: Jewish legal practice was serious and diverse; later rabbinic texts are later comparative witnesses.
hermeneutical_lens.original_audience: Modern readers need protection from antisemitism, food shaming, forced eating, and universalizing one passage.
hermeneutical_lens.genre: Distinguish priestly law, Gospel controversy, vision, council letter, Pauline argument, manuscript variant, and papyrus.
hermeneutical_lens.messianic_christological_trajectory: The New Testament passages relate Jesus and Messiah-confession to holiness and gentile community in distinct ways; CKL does not prescribe one synthesis.
major_interpretive_views: Mark 7:19 narrator comment versus digestive argument
hermeneutical_lens.historical_interpretation: Direct texts and dated comparisons constrain reconstruction but do not decide modern food rules.
hermeneutical_lens.authorial_intent: Each author addresses a particular narrative or communal problem rather than writing a modern diet manual.
hermeneutical_lens.christological_significance: First Corinthians relates the one Lord and Lord's table to idolatry; theological development remains outside historical proof.
